lesson.title: Reading the Symbols: The Integral Sign, dx, and the Ghost of the Sum
lesson.summary: The integral notation with its elongated S and trailing dx is not decoration, it is compact shorthand for the entire limit-of-a-Riemann-sum process, and learning to read it that way makes the symbol far less mysterious.
lesson.body:
The symbol used for a definite integral, written as the integral sign followed by f(x) dx with a and b marked at the bottom and top, looks like it appeared out of nowhere the first time you see it. It did not. The integral sign itself is an elongated letter S, chosen by Leibniz because the definite integral is fundamentally a sum, the limiting value of sum after sum of rectangle areas. The dx at the end is the ghost of delta x, the width of each rectangle in the Riemann sum. As the number of rectangles grows without bound, delta x shrinks toward 0, and dx is the notation for what that shrinking width becomes in the limit. So the full expression, the integral from a to b of f(x) dx, is literally shorthand for the limit as n approaches infinity of the sum from i = 1 to n of f(x_i) times delta x. Every worked Riemann sum limit from the earlier chapters in this sequence is exactly what this notation is standing in for.

The function f(x) written between the integral sign and the dx is called the integrand, the thing being accumulated. It plays the same role as f(x_i) inside the sum, the height sampled at each point. Writing dx at the end still matters even though nothing is literally being multiplied once you have taken the limit, because dx tells you which variable is doing the accumulating. This becomes important later when integrals involve more than one letter, since dx signals unambiguously that x is the variable sweeping across the interval while any other letters in the expression are being treated as fixed.

Here is a worked example that shows the notation and the sum it stands for producing the same number. Let f(x) = 3 - x on [0, 3]. In sum notation, using right endpoints x_i = 3i/n and width delta x = 3/n, the Riemann sum is R_n = sum of (3 - 3i/n) times (3/n) = (3/n) times [3n - (3/n) times the sum of i from 1 to n]. Using sum of i from 1 to n = n(n+1)/2, this becomes R_n = 9 - (9/(2n)) times (n+1) = 9 - 4.5 - 4.5/n = 4.5 - 4.5/n, which approaches 4.5 as n grows without bound. In integral notation, this entire computation is what is meant by writing the integral from 0 to 3 of (3 - x) dx, and it equals 4.5. You can check this geometrically too: the graph of f(x) = 3 - x on [0, 3] is a line from (0, 3) down to (3, 0), forming a right triangle with both legs of length 3, whose area is 1/2 times 3 times 3 = 4.5. All three routes, the raw sum, the compact notation, and plain geometry, agree, which is exactly the point of the notation: it packages an entire limiting process into a symbol you can manipulate without rederiving the sum every time.

One piece of this notation has been glossed over so far: the a and b marking where the accumulation starts and stops. Those are called the limits of integration, and they deserve their own careful treatment, which is exactly where the next chapter picks up.
